1: After he sold them, etc. This implies that if he said so at the time of the sale, he is believed to forbid [the slaughter of the animal on that day]. This is also implied by what the Rosh wrote in the chapter Oto V'et Beno [Chullin, Chapter 5], and these are his words: "I saw it written in the name of Rav Achai that if a gentile merchant is selling animals, one must be concerned with the matter that perhaps he sold the mother today. But it is not logical at all, because it is uncommon, and we do not presume a prohibition as long as the seller did not inform [the buyer], etc., for if there is cause for concern out of doubt, etc." End of quote. This implies that if he informed him at the time of the sale, it is forbidden to slaughter the animal purchased from him on that day. However, it is obvious that if there is reason to believe he is saying this merely to improve his transaction (i.e., as a sales pitch or to inflate its perceived value), his words are meaningless. This is like that which is stated in the last chapter of Yevamot (page 122): "A gentile who sells fruit and says they are orlah [fruit from a tree's first three years]—his words are meaningless." See Section 122, Subsection 6, for more on the laws of a gentile regarding this.
